extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers (gentlemen, coffee-house public) interested in manners, fashion, and domestic conduct
extracted.subtask_short: advice on fashion and married conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Spectator essays offering prescriptive guidance on establishing a fashionable society/registry, selecting its officers and insignia, and on proper conduct in marriage and public life (how to behave, accept honours, and resolve affronts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for Directors of the fashionable Society
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Beaus are to be presented in the first place; include Time-Servers (those who, without conviction or view of interest, change with the World merely from a terror of being out of Fashion); those who, from facility of temper and too much obsequiousness, are vicious against their will and follow leaders whom they do not approve for want of courage; those who are both to grow old, or would do any thing contrary to the Course and Order of things, out of fondness to be in Fashion; and those who are in Fashion without apparent Merit (supposed to have latent Qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect lists of persons qualified for this trust from chief coffee-houses and conversations: each such place may name two or three candidates; submissions requested within fourteen days; the place of the Physician is already engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and motto for the House of Fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is to be a Picture over the Door, with a Looking-Glass and a Dressing-Chair in the Middle of it: on one side above one another, Patch-Boxes, Pin-Cushions, and little Bottles; on the other, Powder Baggs, Puffs, Combs and Brushes; beyond these, Swords with fine Knots (points hidden), and Fans almost closed, with the Handles downward, standing interchangeably from the Sides till they meet at the Top and form a Semicircle; beneath all, the Writing (motto) runs in this pretty sounding Manner: 'Adeste, O quotquot sunt, Veneres, Gratiæ, Cupidines, En vobis adsunt in promptu Faces, Vincula, Spicula, Hinc eligite, sumite, regite.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a learned-language motto and emblematic picture to show respect to Foreigners and to indicate the House's purpose as a finishing place of breeding; the visual program should combine dressing implements and martial/fashion symbols as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and benefits of a Registry of Fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: This Project will be a Registry, to which Posterity may have recourse, for clearing obscure passages in authors about dress; it will free scholars from spending time to describe ancient dresses from dark hints and spare the world useless volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the registry as both a practical reference for contemporary fashion and a scholarly resource that prevents misguided etymological or historical conjectures (e.g., misinterpreting farthingal or furbeloe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection procedure for the Society's directors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the matter is of too much weight for a private man to determine alone, chief coffee-houses (each carried on by a person with followers and admirers) should name two or three persons from among themselves to be inserted; those so named should be put up with great faithfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit nominations from existing social hubs; prioritize public nomination and collective vetting rather than a single private decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a disposition to be pleased in married life
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a Rule proper to be observed in all Occurrences of Life, but more especially in the domestick or matrimonial Part of it, to preserve always a Disposition to be pleased. This cannot be supported but by considering things in their right light, and as Nature has form'd them, and not as our own Fancies or Appetites would have them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect human imperfections (dishumour, age, sickness, impatience, sullenness) in a spouse; temper passion with reason so small faults do not provoke indifference, dislike, or rage; cultivate the habit of finding pleasure in seemingly indifferent things (children's sayings, domestic scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring reason to support passion (husbandly duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Man who brings his Reason to support his Passion, and beholds what he loves as liable to all the Calamities of human Life... will adapt his Mind to the Nature of his Circumstances; he will be prepared to be a Father, a Friend, an Advocate, a Steward for People yet unborn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form your expectations of marriage on realistic grounds and duties (honour, friendship, stewardship) rather than theatrical or romantic imaginings; this temperament yields resilience to noise, cares of children, and ordinary domestic annoyances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience and philosophical forbearance with a 'woman of spirit' (managing a shrew)
rubrics_metrics.description: When perverse Jades fall to men's lots, and are joined to men of warm spirits without temper or learning, they are frequently corrected with Stripes; but... this ought to be used sparingly. Rather recommend... to form themselves for the World by Patience at home. Socrates acknowledged he owed great part of his virtue to the exercise his useful Wife constantly gave it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer patience and the cultivation of personal virtue to harsh corporal correction; bear provocations as opportunities to improve fortitude and temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for accepting honours and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: All Distinctions are useful to Men, only as they are to act in Publick; it would be a romantick Madness for a Man to be a Lord in his Closet. Nothing can be honourable to a Man apart from the World, but the Reflection upon worthy Actions; he that places Honour in a Consciousness of Well-doing, will have but little Relish for any outward Homage that is paid him. Those who accept of Favour without Merit, support themselves in it at the Expence of your Majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept titles and honours only insofar as they enable or reflect public service and conduct; decline honours that would embarrass private habits or that are unsupported by ability and merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper legal/diplomatic remedies for affronts between servants
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Man makes a Mouth at me I am not to knock the Teeth out of it for his Pains. Count Rechteren should have made Affidavit that his Servants had been affronted, and then Monsieur Ménager would have done him Justice, by taking away their Liveries from 'em, or some other way he thought proper; as for Monsieur Ménager, upon his Servants being beaten, he might have had his Action of Assault and Battery. As the case stands... they ought to bring it to Referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal, legal, or arbitral procedures (affidavit, demands for satisfaction, removal of livery, actions for assault and battery, referral to arbitrators) rather than immediate violent reprisals; diplomatic matters should be referred to referees/arbitration to avoid escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not interpret neighbours' afflictions as divine punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be guilty of a greater Act of Uncharitableness, than to interpret the Afflictions which befal our Neighbours, as Punishments and Judgments. This Humour of turning every Misfortune into a Judgment proceeds from wrong Notions of Religion, which... in its own nature, produces Goodwill towards Men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid construing misfortunes as moral judgments; cultivate charity and mild constructions of others' accidents; recognize that religious sentiment should soften, not sour, one's temper toward the afflicted.
